questions.prompt: What primary purpose does view identity serve in SwiftUI?

options.text: It connects temporary view structs to persistent state and dependencies across redraws.
options.explanation: Identity allows SwiftUI to recognize when a newly created struct represents the same logical view.

options.text: It assigns unique IPv6 hardware network addresses to each visual element on screen.
options.explanation: Identity is a SwiftUI layout and state concept, not a network protocol.

options.text: It serializes the entire user interface into encrypted local disk storage.
options.explanation: Identity governs view lifetime and state in memory, not disk serialization.

options.text: It forces views to render exclusively using CPU software graphics rasterization.
options.explanation: Identity has no connection to hardware graphics rasterization engines.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between explicit identity and structural identity?

options.text: Explicit identity uses static view code, while structural identity uses custom UUIDs.
options.explanation: Explicit identity uses custom keys like .id(), while structural identity uses view hierarchy position.

options.text: Explicit identity uses assigned identifiers, while structural identity uses view tree position.
options.explanation: Explicit identity comes from .id() or Identifiable, while structural identity is inferred from code structure.

options.text: Explicit identity is only available in UIKit, while structural identity is used in SwiftUI.
options.explanation: Both forms of identity are core concepts in SwiftUI.

options.text: There is no functional distinction between explicit and structural identity.
options.explanation: They represent fundamentally different ways SwiftUI tracks view nodes.

questions.prompt: What happens to a view @State when its structural identity changes due to an if/else branch switch?

options.text: SwiftUI transfers the state automatically to the alternative branch.
options.explanation: Because the branches have different structural identities, state is not transferred.

options.text: The state is backed up in persistent cache until the branch re-activates.
options.explanation: SwiftUI destroys previous state rather than caching it indefinitely.

options.text: The old state is destroyed and fresh initial state is created for the new branch.
options.explanation: Switching structural identity branches terminates the old view lifetime and resets state.

options.text: The compiler blocks branch switching to protect memory integrity.
options.explanation: Branch switching is supported and standard in SwiftUI view trees.

questions.prompt: Why is using a ternary operator preferred over if/else for toggling view styling?

options.text: The ternary operator forces the Swift compiler to inline all function calls.
options.explanation: Ternary operators do not control compiler function inlining.

options.text: The ternary operator causes views to re-render using Metal shaders.
options.explanation: Ternary expressions do not dictate GPU shader usage.

options.text: The ternary operator prevents child views from declaring local constants.
options.explanation: Child views can declare local variables regardless of ternary operators.

options.text: It preserves a single view identity, retaining internal state and fluid animations.
options.explanation: Ternary modifiers maintain view position and identity, avoiding state destruction and animation breaks.

questions.prompt: Why should developers avoid wrapping view hierarchies in AnyView?

options.text: Type erasure destroys static structural identity, impairing diffing performance.
options.explanation: AnyView hides exact view types and static tree layout, preventing efficient hierarchy diffing.

options.text: AnyView causes an immediate runtime fatal error on iOS 16 and later devices.
options.explanation: AnyView is valid syntax and compiles cleanly, but causes performance degradation.

options.text: AnyView disables touch event delivery across the entire display screen.
options.explanation: Touches are still delivered to AnyView hierarchies.

options.text: AnyView converts Swift structs into Objective-C classes at runtime.
options.explanation: AnyView is a Swift type-erased wrapper, not an Objective-C class bridge.

questions.prompt: What happens if a view calls .id(UUID()) inside its body property?

options.text: SwiftUI deduplicates the identifier to prevent unnecessary view invalidations.
options.explanation: UUID() generates a unique string every time, preventing deduplication.

options.text: A new identity is created on every render pass, destroying state and animations.
options.explanation: Generating dynamic IDs inside body resets view lifetime on every redraw.

options.text: The view hierarchy is cached permanently in memory without redrawing.
options.explanation: Dynamic IDs force constant redraws rather than caching.

options.text: The compiler flags the expression as a fatal type mismatch error.
options.explanation: UUID conforms to Hashable and compiles cleanly with .id().

questions.prompt: How is a view lifetime defined in SwiftUI?
questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview

options.text: The lifespan of the transient View struct instance allocated in memory.
options.explanation: View structs are recreated repeatedly; lifetime refers to identity and state persistence.

options.text: The duration of the application process from launch until termination.
options.explanation: Individual views appear and disappear while the application runs.

options.text: The duration over which SwiftUI associates a persistent identity with state storage.
options.explanation: A view lifetime begins when its identity is added and ends when that identity is removed.

options.text: The time taken by the GPU to render a single display frame buffer.
options.explanation: A single frame render takes milliseconds, whereas view lifetime spans user interactions.

questions.prompt: When does SwiftUI call a view body property to produce a new view value?

options.text: At a fixed rate of precisely sixty times per second continuously.
options.explanation: SwiftUI only evaluates body when an observed dependency changes.

options.text: Only when the device rotates between portrait and landscape modes.
options.explanation: Any state or dependency change triggers body evaluation, not just device rotation.

options.text: Every time the user taps on any non-interactive pixel on the screen.
options.explanation: Taps on non-interactive areas do not trigger body evaluation unless state mutates.

options.text: Whenever an observed dependency such as @State or @Binding mutates.
options.explanation: SwiftUI tracks view dependencies and re-evaluates body when tracked data changes.

questions.prompt: What happens to active .task modifiers when a view identity changes?

options.text: Active tasks attached to the terminated identity are cancelled cooperatively.
options.explanation: Because view lifetime ends when identity changes, attached .task modifiers are cancelled.

options.text: Active tasks are promoted to high-priority global background tasks.
options.explanation: Tasks are cancelled when the view identity leaves the hierarchy.

options.text: Active tasks freeze in memory until the original view re-appears.
options.explanation: Tasks are cancelled, not paused in memory.

options.text: Active tasks continue running and deliver results to the new identity.
options.explanation: Tasks belong to the specific view identity and are cancelled on identity termination.

questions.prompt: How does SwiftUI represent an if/else condition in its internal type system?
questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview

options.text: Using a dynamically dispatched NSArray of untyped closures.
options.explanation: SwiftUI uses strong generic types produced by ViewBuilder.

options.text: Using the generic type _ConditionalContent<TrueContent, FalseContent>.
options.explanation: The ViewBuilder transform converts if/else statements into _ConditionalContent types.

options.text: Using an unmanaged C-style function pointer table.
options.explanation: SwiftUI view composition is built entirely with Swift generic structs.

options.text: Using a mutable dictionary mapping boolean flags to UIViews.
options.explanation: SwiftUI represents hierarchies statically with value types, not UIViews.

questions.prompt: When is assigning an explicit identifier with .id() desirable in application code?

options.text: When you want to prevent a view from ever redrawing its body property.
options.explanation: Assigning an id does not prevent a view from redrawing when dependencies change.

options.text: When you need to convert a SwiftUI struct into an Objective-C class.
options.explanation: The .id() modifier has no role in Objective-C runtime bridging.

options.text: When you want to force state reset and re-trigger entrance transitions explicitly.
options.explanation: Changing the id resets the view lifetime, discarding old state and re-running entrance transitions.

options.text: When you want to disable dark mode support for a specific container.
options.explanation: Dark mode is controlled via color scheme environment values, not .id().

questions.prompt: How does view identity stability impact SwiftUI animation performance?

options.text: Stable identity prevents the GPU from interpolating layout attributes.
options.explanation: Stable identity enables smooth GPU interpolation of changing attributes.

options.text: Unstable identity accelerates animation frames by skipping layout passes.
options.explanation: Unstable identity causes stutter by triggering destructive transitions instead of property animations.

options.text: Identity has no effect on whether animations or transitions execute.
options.explanation: Transitions execute on identity changes, while animations interpolate properties of stable identities.

options.text: Stable identity allows smooth property interpolation, whereas identity changes cause abrupt transitions.
options.explanation: SwiftUI can only animate property changes across frames when the view identity remains identical.

questions.prompt: Why can SwiftUI discard and recreate view structs frequently without losing data?

options.text: Because state storage is managed externally by SwiftUI and tied to view identity.
options.explanation: View structs are descriptions; actual state is stored by the SwiftUI graph using identity.

options.text: Because view structs are automatically pinned to permanent heap addresses.
options.explanation: View structs are value types copied and discarded on the stack.

options.text: Because view properties are converted into global singleton variables.
options.explanation: View properties are local to their struct instances and view graph nodes.

options.text: Because the compiler rewrites struct initializers to return previous instances.
options.explanation: Initializers construct fresh struct values; SwiftUI links state separately.

questions.prompt: Which construct in ForEach provides explicit identity for collection items?

options.text: The index offset parameter passed into the child view closure.
options.explanation: Using array indices as identity causes bugs when items are reordered or removed.

options.text: The id key path parameter or the Identifiable protocol conformance.
options.explanation: ForEach uses an id key path or Identifiable.id to establish explicit identity for each item.

options.text: The memory address of the parent view body closure.
options.explanation: Closure memory addresses do not identify collection elements.

options.text: The system font size environment value of the enclosing container.
options.explanation: Font environment values have no relationship to item identity.

questions.prompt: What issue occurs when using array indices as explicit identity in ForEach?

options.text: The collection cannot contain more than eight elements simultaneously.
options.explanation: There is no collection size limit when using array indices.

options.text: All items in the list become unclickable and ignore gesture taps.
options.explanation: Taps still register, but animations and state will be misattributed.

options.text: Inserting or deleting items causes incorrect animation and state misattribution.
options.explanation: If item 0 is deleted, item 1 inherits index 0, corrupting animations and local state.

options.text: The compiler issues a fatal diagnostic and refuses to compile the view.
options.explanation: ForEach(indices, id: \.self) compiles cleanly despite being error-prone.

questions.prompt: Compare explicit identity and structural identity in SwiftUI, providing a clear example of each.

rubric.criterion: Defines explicit identity as custom assigned identifiers such as .id() or Identifiable
Defines structural identity as inferred by SwiftUI based on the view position in the code hierarchy
Provides clear code examples illustrating both forms of identity

questions.modelAnswer: Explicit identity uses custom identifiers assigned by the developer, such as calling `.id(item.uuid)` or conforming models to `Identifiable` in a `ForEach`. Structural identity is inferred automatically by SwiftUI based on the view's static position within the hierarchy tree. For example, an `if/else` block creates two structural identities because each branch occupies a distinct position in the layout graph.

questions.prompt: Explain what a view lifetime is in SwiftUI and what occurs when a view identity changes.

rubric.criterion: Defines view lifetime as the period over which SwiftUI links an identity to persistent state storage
Explains that changing identity terminates the previous lifetime and destroys its @State storage
Notes that active .task modifiers are cancelled and fresh initial state is allocated for the new identity

questions.modelAnswer: A view lifetime in SwiftUI is the duration for which SwiftUI associates a persistent identity with allocated state storage. When a view identity changes or leaves the hierarchy, its lifetime ends. SwiftUI destroys the previous `@State` storage, cancels any running `.task` modifiers cooperatively, and allocates fresh default state for the newly introduced view identity.

questions.prompt: Why is using a ternary operator preferred over an if/else block when updating a view style?

rubric.criterion: Explains that ternary operators maintain a single stable view identity
Points out that if/else creates two distinct structural identities that destroy and reset @State
Notes that stable identity allows smooth animation of property changes across frames

questions.modelAnswer: Using a ternary operator preserves a single structural identity for the view, modifying only a property value across render passes. This maintains internal `@State` and enables smooth animation interpolation. In contrast, an `if/else` block creates two distinct structural identities. This forces SwiftUI to terminate the view lifetime, discard existing state, and show abrupt transitions.

questions.prompt: Why does using AnyView degrade performance in complex SwiftUI view hierarchies?

rubric.criterion: Explains that AnyView performs type erasure on the underlying concrete view types
Explains that type erasure hides the static hierarchy structure from the diffing algorithm
Notes that this forces SwiftUI to destroy and recreate views rather than updating existing nodes

questions.modelAnswer: `AnyView` performs type erasure on concrete view types, hiding the compile-time structural tree from SwiftUI. Because the layout engine cannot inspect the static hierarchy structure, its diffing algorithm cannot determine whether a node merely changed properties. This forces SwiftUI to destroy and recreate view nodes and state on render passes, causing dropped frames in complex hierarchies.

questions.prompt: Explain what happens when a developer attaches .id(UUID()) to a view inside its body property.

rubric.criterion: Explains that UUID() generates a fresh unique identifier on every single body evaluation pass
Explains that this forces SwiftUI to treat the view as a completely new identity on each redraw
Mentions that all @State is wiped, animations break, and tasks re-execute continually

questions.modelAnswer: Calling `.id(UUID())` inside a view `body` creates a new unique identifier on every single evaluation pass. Because the identity changes on every redraw, SwiftUI treats the view as a brand new element. This continuously wipes all local `@State` storage, cancels and restarts `.task` modifiers, and breaks smooth animation transitions, severely degrading performance.
